title: Temperature Controlled Environments in an Abattoir

lessons.title: The cold chain inside the abattoir
lessons.html:
Where temperature control is needed

From the moment an animal is slaughtered, its meat is at risk from bacteria. Temperature control slows bacterial growth. The cold chain is the unbroken series of cold areas that meat passes through until it reaches the customer. The Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and its regulations require abattoirs to keep meat at safe temperatures; the exact limits for each area are set in the abattoir's hygiene management plan and procedures.

Temperature-controlled areas

AreaPurpose
Carcass chillersBring warm carcasses down to the required deep muscle temperature
Offal chillersCool red offal quickly; offal spoils faster than carcasses
Holding chillersKeep chilled carcasses cold until dispatch
FreezersFreeze meat for storage, or for conditional treatment where the regulations allow
Deboning and cutting roomsKept cool so meat does not warm up while it is handled
Dispatch bay and vehiclesPrevent warming while meat is loaded and transported

What affects chilling

  • Loading: too many warm carcasses in one chiller overload the cooling system.
  • Spacing: carcasses must not touch, so cold air flows around them.
  • Air movement: fans must work and must not be blocked.
  • Door discipline: doors left open let warm, moist air in, causing condensation.
  • Carcass size: heavy beef hindquarters take longer to chill than lamb carcasses.

Condensation

Warm moist air meeting cold surfaces forms drops of water that drip onto meat and carry bacteria. Report condensation on ceilings, rails and pipes above meat immediately so it can be wiped and the cause corrected.

lessons.title: Monitoring, recording and corrective action
lessons.html:
How temperatures are monitored

During your work experience you will help check and record temperatures. Two types of temperature are measured:

  • Room (air) temperature in each chiller and freezer, shown on a display or recorded by a data logger.
  • Product (deep muscle) temperature, measured with a probe thermometer in the thickest part of the carcass or in a carton of offal.

Using a probe thermometer

  1. Check that the thermometer is calibrated; many abattoirs check probes regularly in iced water and record the result.
  2. Clean and sanitise the probe before and after each use.
  3. Insert it into the centre of the thickest muscle, not into fat or touching bone.
  4. Wait until the reading is steady.
  5. Record the carcass number, time, reading and your name.

Monitoring schedule

Follow the schedule in your abattoir's procedure, for example at the start of shift, at set times during the day, and before dispatch. Electronic loggers record continuously, but someone must still check them and act on alarms.

When a temperature is out of limit

  1. Report to the supervisor straight away.
  2. Find the cause: door left open, overloaded chiller, failed fan or compressor, power failure.
  3. Protect the product: stop loading more warm carcasses into that chiller, move meat to another chiller if there is space.
  4. Record the problem, the action and the time.
  5. Product that may have been at unsafe temperatures is held until the veterinarian or quality manager decides what to do with it.

Safety in cold rooms

Wear warm protective clothing. Check that the inside door release works so nobody can be locked in. Never stay alone in a freezer for long periods; tell someone where you are. Floors may be icy, so walk carefully.

Key points

  • The cold chain must not be broken from chiller to customer.
  • Measure both room temperature and deep muscle temperature.
  • Use a calibrated, sanitised probe in the thickest muscle.
  • Report and record any out-of-limit temperature and hold suspect product.
  • Check the inside door release of cold rooms and never work alone in a freezer for long.
